newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australian retailers see cheerier end to 1996.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australian retailers see cheerier end to 1996.

text.p: With Christmas less than two weeks away, Australia's retailers are expected to have a more festive season than last year even though it will be largely driven by stock controls rather than by busy turnstiles.

"The fall in the unemployment rate in November, along with the cut in official interest rates, should provide a boost to consumer confidence and increase the willingness of consumers to spend over the Christmas period," Nomura Research senior economist Andrew Pease said.
But others are not so sure.
While the surprise announcement of another interest rate cut and a fall in the unemployment rate may lift consumer confidence, it may have come too late for a large upswing in Christmas spending.
"Christmas on the demand side is going to be pretty weak," said one analyst, who did not want to be named.
"On the margin side, there is discounting occurring but we do not believe it is as severe as it was this time last year."
Retailers and analysts welcomed last week's surprise interest rate cut by the Reserve Bank, which lowered the official cash rate to 6.0 percent from 6.5 percent.
The reduction will have a positive impact on the sector in 1997, they said.
"Obviously the headlines have been favourable," Citibank Australia chief economist Stephen Koukoulas.
Christmas is a crucial time for retailers, accounting for 25-40 percent of annual profits for some.

The two largest retailers, Woolworths Ltd and Coles Myer Ltd told Reuters there are good signs emerging for the 1996 Christmas trade and both expect, if trends continued, to be able to do better than in 1995.
Retailers were disappointed last year, with Christmas 1995 substantially weaker than most had hoped and forcing stores to conducted big January discount sales.

Debra Stirling, general manager public affairs for Coles Meyer, said the group has been much more cautious in 1996. "Therefore we are not in a situation where we are heavily overstocked and we need to shift products at discount prices," she said.

Woolworths group managing director Reg Clairs said his company has also taken a cautiously optimistic approach and while the dollar value of stocks is higher, because Woolworths has more stores, its number of days' stock is slightly down.
Analysts said although some sectors, such as apparels, appear to be overstocked and are subject to discounting, it does not seem to be as widespread as last year.
Economists said the outlook for retail trade has improved in the last couple of months, and while the December quarter may finish as a weak quarter, performance should improve in 1997.

Citibank's Koukoulas said a change in spending patterns occurred in the recession with consumers deliberately standing back until the start of the post-Christmas sales. He said this pattern may keep the December figure on the weak side unless the Australian Bureau of Statistics has made an allowance for it in the seasonal adjustment factors.
Retailers and brokers agreed customers are becoming more value conscious generally but played down concerns that they were tending to shop for the next Christmas in January.
"This has been a trend which has been going on for many many years, but no-one had actually surveyed it before," Clairs said.
"I think what people wait until after Christmas to buy is the new shirt or new tie or new dress...but people do not wait until January 1 to buy their turkey," he said.
-- Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
